subject: Computer Networking
title: DNS: Naming the Internet
description: Learn DNS: Naming the Internet in one minute.

hook.text: Early ARPANET had a single file listing every host and its address. By the 1980s, that file was unmanageable.

buildup.text: Paul Mockapetris invented DNS in 1983 — a distributed system that could scale to millions of names.

discovery.text: DNS uses a tree structure: root at the top, then .com, .org, .edu, then individual domain names below.

twist.text: Before DNS, adding a host meant editing a shared text file and waiting for it to propagate. Manual and slow.

climax.text: DNS made the internet usable. Imagine typing 142.250.80.46 instead of google.com every single time.

punchline.text: DNS gave the internet human-friendly names.

quiz.question: What problem did DNS solve?
options: A single host file couldn't scale to millions of addresses
Packets were arriving out of order
Email couldn't be sent between different networks

details.summary: The Domain Name System, introduced in 1983, replaced a single hosts file with a distributed hierarchical database for translating domain names to IP addresses. Created by Paul Mockapetris, DNS made the internet usable by allowing people to use memorable names instead of numeric addresses.
details.whyItMatters: DNS made the internet human-friendly. Without it, you would need to memorize numeric IP addresses for every website. DNS is the foundation of how people navigate the internet.
takeaways: DNS replaced a manually maintained hosts file in 1983
It distributes name resolution across a hierarchy of servers
DNS made the internet navigable with human-readable names

faq.question: What did DNS replace?
faq.answer: Before DNS, a single text file called HOSTS.TXT mapped hostnames to addresses. It was maintained centrally and distributed to all computers. As the network grew, this file became unmanageable. DNS distributed the responsibility across a hierarchy of authoritative servers.

faq.question: How does the DNS hierarchy work?
faq.answer: Root servers direct queries to top-level domain servers like .com or .org. TLD servers direct queries to authoritative servers for specific domains. Each level only needs to know about the next level down, making the system scalable to billions of domain names.
